analysis.one_liner: Bans states from requiring GMO labels on food and sets up a voluntary federal certification program instead.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 275-150 in July 2015, but the Senate never voted and it died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have kept GMO food labeling voluntary at the federal level and blocked states from requiring companies to disclose genetically engineered ingredients on packaging. It would have continued the FDA's voluntary industry consultation process as the safety gate, created a voluntary USDA program for companies that want to label food non-GMO, and preempted state and local GMO labeling rules — including laws like Vermont's that had already passed. It also would have defined the term 'natural' on food labels and preempted state rules on that word.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that sell genetically engineered crops and packaged foods made with them. They would avoid the cost and reputational risk of mandatory on-package GMO disclosure, and instead of facing state-by-state labeling rules, they would face one national standard with no mandatory label.

how_it_helps.text: The bill preempts any state or local requirement for labeling genetically engineered food, so no state could force companies to put GMO information on packages [S2][S3][S5].

It keeps the FDA's existing voluntary consultation process as the safety review: a GMO food could only be sold after FDA raised no objection to the developer's own safety determination, which the bill makes enforceable through USDA's registry [S3][S5].

It creates a national voluntary certification program so companies that want to market food as non-GMO can do so under uniform USDA standards, with certified organic products automatically deemed non-GMO [S3][S5].
It requires the FDA to write regulations defining when companies may use the word 'natural' on food labels, a term that had no federal definition [S2][S5].

analysis.who_pays: Shoppers who want to know whether their food contains genetically engineered ingredients. The bill declares that genetic engineering alone is not a 'material difference' the FDA must disclose, so the label would only appear if the FDA found a difference in the food itself — meaning most GMO foods would carry no disclosure at all.

drawbacks.text: A supporter would argue GMO foods on the market are as safe as comparable foods, and the bill requires FDA sign-off before any GMO food can be sold, so the safety gate remains [S3][S5].
A national standard does avoid a patchwork of conflicting state rules for companies selling food in every state.

But the bill's core effect is to strip states of the power to require disclosure: it preempts state and local GMO labeling laws and says genetic engineering by itself is never a material difference justifying a label, so the disclosure shoppers ask for would almost never appear on the package [S3][S5].
It also bars labels or advertising from suggesting non-GMO foods are safer or of higher quality than GMO foods, restricting what producers who market non-GMO food can say [S3][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's one real upside — a single national rule instead of fifty state rules — comes at the cost of the very disclosure most states' residents were seeking: it removes mandatory GMO labels entirely rather than replacing them with a national version. The safety provisions it does add formalize a process where the developer's own determination, not independent FDA testing, is the basis for approval. Weighed honestly, the bill's main work is to end the state labeling movement, and that benefit flows to food and seed companies, not to shoppers.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 275-150 on July 23, 2015, but after the Senate referred it to its Agriculture Committee the next day, the committee never brought it up and no Senate vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Pompeo (R-KS) introduced the bill on March 25, 2015, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Agriculture Committees [S1][S7].
The House Agriculture Committee reported the bill as amended on July 16, 2015 [S3][S7].
During floor debate on July 23, 2015, amendments from Reps. DeFazio, Huffman, DeLauro, and Pingree — each aiming to add disclosure requirements — were all rejected [S7].
The House passed the bill 275-150 (Roll no. 462), with 230 of 245 Republicans voting yes and 138 of 188 Democrats voting no [S8][S7].

The Senate received the bill on July 24, 2015, and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which took no action; no Senate vote occurred before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5][S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers who want GMO disclosure, and the state governments whose labeling laws the bill would have wiped out. Because the Senate never acted, states kept the power to require labeling and companies kept the underlying state-labeling risk the bill was designed to remove.

sides.party_line_note: On final passage, 230 of 245 House Republicans voted yes while only 45 of 188 Democrats did — the bill passed with nearly unanimous Republican support and strong Democratic opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have guaranteed no mandatory on-package GMO disclosure anywhere in the country, and would have barred states from ever imposing one. Its core label provision declares genetic engineering alone is never a 'material difference' requiring disclosure, which is exactly the outcome the industry sought. [S3][S5]

Mandatory state GMO labeling laws would have required segregated supply chains, testing, and separate labels by state. A single national voluntary standard eliminates those compliance costs — and the consumer-facing label. [S2][S5]

industries.industry: Certified organic and non-GMO food producers
industries.note: The bill creates a national voluntary non-GMO certification program and deems certified organic products non-GMO, but it also bars producers from suggesting non-GMO food is safer or higher quality, constraining their marketing claims. [S3][S5]
